episode_title: Nationalism Is Bad for the Nation

stories.topic: The India-Pakistan cricket match that sparked this episode
stories.summary: The day after India played Pakistan in a recent tournament, Amit scrolled through Twitter and was deeply disturbed. Indian players had refused to shake hands with the Pakistani team. The captain and politicians made belligerent noises at press conferences, and social media erupted after India won. India had the far stronger team, and any knockout game has an element of lottery. Indian and Pakistani cricketers have historically been friendly, and Pakistani commentators like Wasim Akram, Waqar Younis and Ramiz Raja are hugely popular in India. Vaishnav, the show's cinematographer, told Amit he couldn't sleep properly after seeing it.
stories.insight: A single sporting moment showed how quickly a whole country can be roused to hate people it has never met. It also showed how easily people confuse the citizens of Pakistan with the Pakistani state, whose interests run opposite to theirs.
stories.quote: for a common person to feel nationalistic, you are doing what Doug Stanhope once described as hating people you have never met and taking pride in accomplishments you had nothing to do with

stories.topic: The Wars of the Roses and the birth of 'Englishness'
stories.summary: Some historians date English national consciousness to the 15th-century Wars of the Roses. The dynastic civil war wiped out many feudal overlords, and with them went the local loyalty that people had owed those lords. Both sides also put commoners and royals into battle together. That created a new shared feeling: I'm a commoner, you're a royal, but we are the same people.
stories.insight: Nations are not primordial. A sense of nationhood can emerge as an accidental side effect of war, once the old local loyalties collapse and something larger fills the gap.
stories.quote: one of the side effects of the dynastic civil war is that a lot of the feudal overlords lost their power. And the local allegiance that you had to a feudal overlord was no longer there because a feudal overlord wasn't there.

stories.topic: Mussolini's 'trenchocracy' and the ghost of Rome
stories.summary: Mussolini rose to power in the early 1920s, just after World War One. He rallied Italians by promising rule by the 'trenchocracy', the common men who had fought in the war. He also exploited Italy's link to the Roman Empire: look how glorious we were, look how far we have fallen, let us rise again. He used pomp, grandeur, and talk of Roman military valour and discipline. Through his disastrous reign he stayed supremely popular.
stories.insight: Nationalist strongmen often don't need coercion at first. A narrative of lost glory makes people walk into disaster willingly.
stories.quote: He didn't even need to be authoritarian in that sense. The people were with him because this was such a popular narrative.

stories.topic: Stalin, Pushkin, and Russia's unbroken nationalist thread
stories.summary: The Tsars used Russification and Russian nationalism to bolster their legitimacy. The communists initially railed against nationalism: 'workers of the world unite', not workers of Russia. After Lenin, though, Stalin brought Russification back. At a 1937 celebration of the Soviet Union's great poets, the poet celebrated most was the Russian, Pushkin. The same strain now runs through Putin's imperial project.
stories.insight: Ideologies that claim to transcend the nation, like class-war communism, slide back into nationalism, because both work the same way: build an in-group and paint everyone else as the enemy.
stories.quote: In nineteen thirty seven there is a celebration of great poets of the Soviet Union. But the one who is celebrated the most is the Russian poet Pushkin.

stories.topic: How Gandhi's Khilafat gambit turned Jinnah
stories.summary: Gandhi returned from South Africa around 1914. His hero Gokhale told him to spend a year travelling India without doing active politics, then died a month later. Gandhi kept the promise, and travelled barefoot as a tribute ('I don't know what the logic of that is'). At Congress gatherings around 1917-18 nobody took him seriously. His breakthrough came when he joined the Ali brothers' Khilafat movement, which wanted the caliphate revived after its abolition at the end of WWI. An Indian independence movement had no coherent reason to ally with a pan-Islamic one, but the tactical masterstroke let Gandhi take over the Congress around 1920-21. Jinnah, then the last great moderate and expecting to lead Congress, couldn't make sense of it. Embittered, he abandoned moderation and became the biggest champion of a Muslim nation.
stories.insight: Borders and nationalisms that look eternal can come from accidents of history: a promise to a dying mentor, an opportunistic alliance, one man's bitterness.
stories.quote: There's no coherent reason for them to come together, but they do. And it proves to be a tactical master stroke because Gandhi takes over the Congress because of this

stories.topic: Acing Hindi exams by stringing together Shudh Hindi
stories.summary: In both 10th and 12th standard Amit scored more in Hindi than in English, despite being 'lazy as fuck' and not studying. His hack was to memorise lots of Shudh Hindi words (dwar instead of darwaza, mitra instead of dost) and string them together. Teachers rewarded it because nobody actually speaks that way.
stories.insight: The Sanskritised, de-Persianised 'pure' Hindi taught in schools is a political construction rather than the living language. The education system rewards the artificial register over the Hindustani people actually speak.
stories.quote: my hack for Hindi was to learn a lot of Shudh Hindi words and then string them together. So even the teacher would say that just give this motherfucker marks. Because nobody speaks in Shudh Hindi.

stories.topic: Neeraj Chopra's mother: 'Arshad is our son too'
stories.summary: When Neeraj Chopra won javelin gold two Olympics ago, he praised Pakistan's Arshad Nadeem, a close friend he had always encouraged, almost like a mentor. At the last Olympics Arshad won gold with an outlier throw of over 92 metres, and a disappointed Neeraj didn't. A TV crew asked Neeraj's mother how she felt. She said Arshad was her son too.
stories.insight: This is the antidote to state-manufactured enmity: people who actually know the 'other side' see them as family. Amit's point is that Indians and Pakistanis are 'the same damn people' with the same culture.
stories.quote: Frankly, we are the same damn people here. It's the same damn culture.

stories.summary: In 1969 Honduras and El Salvador played a series of World Cup qualifiers marked by so much sloganeering and fighting that a war followed. Amit recalls it lasting about 100 days, with around six thousand dead. It is commonly called the Soccer War.
stories.insight: Sport doesn't cause these conflicts; nationalism does. Sport is just an easy trigger and amplifier for passions already stoked.
stories.quote: And it is not that soccer caused the war. Nationalism caused the war, but soccer was the trigger.

stories.topic: Shubha Mudgal's sigh about renamed ragas
stories.summary: On The Seen and the Unseen, Amit suggested to Shubha Mudgal that nationalism surely couldn't touch music, since Hindustani classical music owes so much to great Muslim performers. She sighed and told him he'd be surprised: there is revisionist history in music too, including attempts by some people to rename ragas.
stories.insight: Nationalist re-coding reaches even art forms whose lineage is plainly multicultural.
stories.quote: And she kind of sighed and she said, You know, you would really be surprised that, you know, even in music there is a revisionist history kind of happening, a renaming of ragas being attempted by some people

stories.topic: The friend who wouldn't let his sister wear salwar kameez
stories.summary: A Kashmiri Pandit, once a close friend of Amit's, told him he didn't let his sister wear salwar kameez because he saw it as something Muslims wear. When Amit grew up in the 70s and 80s, salwar kameez on women was widely frowned upon as 'Muslim'; today it is completely normal. The pathani suit Amit wears on the show would still be read by many as Eid-wear or a sign that you're Muslim.
stories.insight: Clothes have no religion, but identity politics assigns them one. Those labels are arbitrary, and they can flip within a generation.
stories.quote: Clothes don't have religion. But the dress I am wearing would be termed as Muslim by many people, which is absolutely terrible.

recommendations.creator: Benedict Anderson
recommendations.context: Amit's opening answer to Ajay's request to define nationalism.
recommendations.reason: Possibly his favourite book on nationalism. It supplies the episode's core definition (a nation is an 'imagined political community', necessarily limited and sovereign) and the three paradoxes of nationhood.

recommendations.creator: W. E. H. Lecky
recommendations.context: Explaining how our tribal instincts gradually widened into loyalty to larger communities.
recommendations.reason: Source of the 'expanding circle': the idea that the circle of people we grant moral consideration widens over time, from family to tribe to village and beyond.

recommendations.creator: Peter Singer
recommendations.reason: Singer argued the circle would one day include animals. Amit's wry note: 'Alas, it hasn't even expanded to include all human beings.'

recommendations.item: The Ferment of Our Founders (Episode 272, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Kapila
recommendations.context: Discussing how nationalisms invent a history to justify themselves.
recommendations.reason: Source of Kapila's line that Hindutva is 'a theory of violence in search of a history'.

recommendations.creator: Manu Pillai
recommendations.context: Explaining how a pan-Hindu identity emerged in India.
recommendations.reason: Documents how Vaishnavites once fought Shaivites more than they fought Muslims, and how a shared Hindu identity formed gradually, first against Islam and then against the British.

recommendations.creator: Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore
recommendations.context: Discussing whether anti-colonial nationalism is a force for good.
recommendations.reason: A 'beautiful book' laying out the Gandhi-Tagore debate: Gandhi as a soft nationalist, Tagore holding the view Amit and Ajay hold today, that nationalism is simply bad.

recommendations.creator: Rabindranath Tagore
recommendations.context: Tagore's lectures from 1917, which Amit quotes at length in the Tagore chapter.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it 'awesome' and urges listeners to read Tagore's full arguments. He applauds Tagore's prescience a century ago, from a man who supported Indian independence yet saw nationalism as toxic whoever wielded it.

recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: Describing the late-80s/early-90s moment when it seemed the world was entering a better age.
recommendations.reason: Captures the brief hope that liberalism had won before nationalism's revival. Amit points out the question mark at the end of the original essay's title.

recommendations.item: Gita Press and the Making of Hindu India
recommendations.creator: Akshaya Mukul
recommendations.context: Arguing that the secular idea of India was imposed top-down while society held different ideas.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a masterpiece that shows how deeply Hindu nationalist ideas were embedded in Indian society.

recommendations.item: The Gita Press and Hindu Nationalism (Episode 139, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Akshaya Mukul
recommendations.reason: Amit's 'great episode' with Mukul, a conversational route into the same argument.

recommendations.creator: George Orwell
recommendations.context: The chapter on how nationalism invades everyday life, starting with sport.
recommendations.reason: The 'great essay' that called sport 'war minus the shooting', drawing on an ugly football match involving a Moscow team and a riot in Spain. It frames the India-Pakistan cricket episode.

recommendations.creator: Vaishnav Vyas
recommendations.context: Explaining that he supports football teams for their playing philosophy, not tribal loyalty.
recommendations.reason: Amit and Vaishnav bond over the thinkers of the game (like Guardiola turning 'anti-Guardiola'). The newsletter models loving sport for ideas rather than flags.

recommendations.item: The Life and Music of Shubha Mudgal (Episode 426, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shubha Mudgal
recommendations.reason: 'My great episode with her', in which Mudgal reveals revisionist history and attempts to rename ragas in Hindustani classical music.

recommendations.context: Example of communities forming around shared tastes rather than national identity.
recommendations.reason: The band has a cult following that forms its own community. Amit tells Ajay 'we will introduce you to some good music.'

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything episode on Understanding Labels
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recalled while distinguishing nationalism from patriotism and the national interest.
recommendations.reason: 'One of my favorite episodes': it unpacks what labels like liberal and conservative really mean, including why nationalism differs from patriotism.

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything episode on Fallacies
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Explaining that our tribal instincts evolved in prehistoric times.
recommendations.reason: Shows how fallacies like zero-sum thinking evolved for tribal life and don't fit the modern world.

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything episode 'Everything Is Indian, Nothing Is Indian'
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.reason: One of the show's most popular episodes. It shows that most 'Indian' food came from outside, so getting nationalistic about it is ridiculous.

recommendations.item: Everything is Everything two-parter on globalization and tariffs
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Setting up the discussion of economic nationalism.
recommendations.reason: Covers how beautiful globalization is and how tariffs harm a country's own people.

core_ideas.concept: Nationalism is not patriotism or the national interest
core_ideas.explanation: Three things often get conflated. The national interest is what is good for your country. Patriotism is love for your country. Nationalism is an ideology, and Amit regards it as toxic. His thesis: nationalism is bad for the nation, any nationalism, any nation.
core_ideas.quote: The national interest is what is good for your country, what is good for the state. Patriotism is love for your country. Nationalism is an ideology that I largely tend to think of as kind of toxic.

core_ideas.concept: Two Pakistans: the people vs the state
core_ideas.explanation: Pakistan's civil society is distinct from what Pranay Kotasthane calls its military-jihadi complex. The Pakistani state draws legitimacy from painting India as the enemy and uses that to oppress its own people. Hostility toward ordinary Pakistanis therefore serves the very state that oppresses them.
core_ideas.quote: In fact, the Pakistani state gets a lot of its legitimacy and power from constantly painting India as an enemy.

core_ideas.concept: Tribal instincts and the expanding circle
core_ideas.explanation: Nationalism is modern but rides on primordial instincts. We evolved in small hunter-gatherer tribes where solidarity with your group and suspicion of outsiders was selected for. Lecky's 'expanding circle' describes how moral concern widens over time from kin to tribe to village to larger communities. The nation is one stage of that widening, and it can freeze there.
core_ideas.quote: And we evolved in those times to be tribalistic.

core_ideas.concept: A nation is an imagined political community
core_ideas.explanation: In Benedict Anderson's definition, a nation is necessarily imagined. Unlike a Dunbar-sized tribe of about 150, you never meet most members or know their preferences, yet you picture them as one homogeneous 'we'. That makes the nation fictional at its heart, and it flattens real complexity: Hinduism, for instance, was an amorphous, almost open-source religion. Anderson adds that a nation must be limited (bounded) and sovereign to make sense.
core_ideas.quote: We don't actually know everybody in this imagined community. We haven't met them. We don't even know their preferences by and large, but we imagine it to be something which we define narrowly, in a necessarily homogeneous way.

core_ideas.explanation: First, objective modernity vs subjective antiquity: nation-states are a few centuries old, yet each claims a glorious ancient past, which has to be invented (Hobsbawm's 'invention of tradition'; Kapila's 'a theory of violence in search of a history'). Second, universal vs particular: everyone supposedly has a nationality, yet each one is unique and potentially hostile to the others. Third, nationalism is a huge political force but philosophically nebulous.
core_ideas.quote: nations per se, especially when we talk of nation states, are a relatively modern concept. They're only a few centuries old. And yet all nations to justify themselves to talk of themselves as a nation will talk about a glorious past.

core_ideas.concept: Nationalism has no serious thinkers, only rationalisations
core_ideas.explanation: Liberalism has Locke and Smith; socialism has Marx. Ajay pushes back that Mussolini had theory, and we just refuse to take him seriously. Amit's reply: Mussolini, Hitler and Savarkar (with his 'motherland and holy land' test) offer assertions, not first-principles reasoning. They are men of action, and their worldview is a rationalisation for what they are doing.
core_ideas.quote: And to me you don't qualify as a serious thinker unless you can tell me the why.

core_ideas.concept: What made nationalism possible, and what revives it
core_ideas.explanation: In medieval Europe loyalties were local, and without maps or printing people barely conceived of a wider world. Several things changed that. Revived vernaculars (French, German) gave people a shared marker. The printing press scaled narratives. Locke and Rousseau's 'will of the people' needed a 'people' to attach to. The Romantic movement, reacting against the Enlightenment's cold rationality, supplied folk songs and fairy tales to rally around. The American and French Revolutions fused these. By the end of the 19th century nationalism ruled the world, and imperialism was nationalism projected outward, with anti-colonial nationalisms rising in response. Social media is today's printing press.
core_ideas.quote: one of my theories for the revival and exacerbation of modern nationalism is that social media enables that kind of primitive tribalism which, you know, you and I twenty years ago would have thought that we're moving away from.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay contrasts landed, culturally conservative people with the commercial, cosmopolitan people of capitalism, like Gujarati traders who sailed off to work across East Africa. Amit thinks nationalism is more about people than land. Ajay locates the overlap in obsession over territory: the cosmopolitan sees the Louisiana or Alaska Purchase as sensible deals, while the nationalist would excoriate any transaction involving land.
core_ideas.quote: Think about it as obsession around territory. That's a land way of thinking. Whereas a more relaxed approach to lines on maps and borders is a part of the cosmopolitan outlook.

core_ideas.concept: The yin and yang of nationalism
core_ideas.explanation: Each claimed good has a matching harm. Liberation vs oppression: nationalism unites the colonised, but every oppressor uses it, and Carl Schmitt said politics needs an other. Cohesion vs exclusion: it bonds people, but every 'we' others a 'them'. Cultural pride vs cultural suppression: it can revive a culture, but declaring A to be 'ours' implies X, Y and Z aren't. Amit's verdict is that the goods can come from elsewhere (liberal self-governance, cities, shared tastes), while the harms are built in.
core_ideas.quote: So you don't actually need to invent a shared identity to do it. You know, you can figure out many good reasons to do it.

core_ideas.explanation: Pride belongs to things you actually did, or helped shape. You can love Kishori Amonkar, Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan and Van Morrison without any narrative of nationhood. 'Taking pride' in your nation's accomplishments is taking credit for what you had nothing to do with.
core_ideas.quote: pride is something you have got to have done something.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's deepest objection. Nationalism, like other identity ideologies, ties you to an accident of birth or location and declares it the most important thing about you. That makes you forever a victim, forever an oppressor, or forever bound to the tribe's dictates. It denies agency and the multitudes every individual contains.
core_ideas.quote: You are tying me down to an identity of birth or location, and you are telling me this is who you are. This is the most important thing about you. Baaki sab jaaye bhaad mein. And I object to this because I feel this dehumanizes me.

core_ideas.concept: The magic trick: how the state turns citizens into subjects
core_ideas.explanation: In Ajay's public-choice view the people are the principal and the state is their hired agent, there to produce public goods and get kicked around when it underperforms. Nationalism inverts this by blurring 'Italy' the football team, 'Italy' the people, and 'Italy' the state that monopolises violence. The state then claims to be the nation, and dissent becomes 'anti-national'. Mussolini said it outright: 'It is not the people who make the state, but the state that makes the people.'
core_ideas.quote: Because once you say nationalism, you've blurred the lines between the people of Italy and the Italian government. And now suddenly the Italian government lays claim to the idea that they represent Italy.

core_ideas.concept: Nationalists pour their own people into war
core_ideas.explanation: Whatever the route, the nationalism of Mussolini, Hitler and Putin ended in mobilising their own people for violence. Ajay notes that something like ten to thirty percent of these countries' men were killed in war. Amit adds that our hardwiring makes this a battle each generation must fight again.
core_ideas.quote: What worse destruction of the people could you achieve other than building this cauldron of war and pouring your own people into the war?

core_ideas.concept: India's top-down 'idea of India' was bound to fail
core_ideas.explanation: Three nationalisms competed under the British: Hindutva (homogenising, aimed at Muslims more than the British), Muslim nationalism (which became Pakistan), and the elite secular nationalism of Nehru, Gandhi and Patel. Amit argues all three are equally imagined, and that every nationalism is imposed through coercion. The secular one won formally but was imposed from the top, while society held other ideas (see the Gita Press). Ambedkar called the constitution a mere topsoil, and Gandhi insisted change must come bottom-up. A smug westernised elite didn't take that seriously, and 'politics has caught up with society.'
core_ideas.quote: But people like us failed because we could not do it from the bottom up.

core_ideas.concept: Hindustani: a spontaneous order split by politics
core_ideas.explanation: North India's language grew bottom-up as a khichdi of Persian, Sanskrit, Prakrit and many tongues now dismissed as dialects ('a language is a dialect with an army'). Then politics intervened: post-1857 British divide-and-rule plus movements within both religions. Urdu was painted as Muslim, and a de-Persianised Hindi was consciously constructed and promoted. Yet the two remain mutually intelligible, and many great writers saw themselves as both Hindi and Urdu writers.
core_ideas.quote: language through spontaneous order in this beautiful bottom up way is a khichdi of different influences.

core_ideas.explanation: Sport is inherently tribal. Indians who've never been to England pick Manchester United or Liverpool, often whichever team was winning when they were 12 or 13. Any team is a Ship of Theseus whose players keep being bought and sold, so loyalty to the badge makes little sense. Amit's alternative is to follow the thinkers of the game and back teams whose style of play you admire.
core_ideas.quote: I support the football teams I support because of playing philosophy.

core_ideas.concept: Economic nationalism is protectionism wearing a flag
core_ideas.explanation: Every voluntary trade is positive-sum, a 'double thank you', whether with Pune or Poland. 'Indian company' barely means anything: ICICI Bank is about 90% foreign-owned, and Infosys has mostly foreign shareholders and customers. Data-localisation rules force data centres into India's heat, unreliable power, thin pool of top-end engineers and tariff-inflated equipment, when Greenland would be cheaper and greener. 'Data is the new crude oil' is just cover for firms that want to avoid competition. The legitimate exception is defence, and even there the fix is foreign policy (e.g. sourcing components from countries like Ukraine), not costly self-reliance.
core_ideas.quote: most of the time what's going on is the firms want to cry mummy and get a government to support them when they are not able to succeed on their own steam.

core_ideas.concept: Nationalism diminishes us in three ways
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's closing case rests on consequences, not first principles. Economically: protectionism makes only us poorer. Culturally and intellectually: we should let all the world's rivers flow into our ocean, and build our own cocktail of Indic and Enlightenment values rather than choosing sides. In character: sorting people into 'ours' and 'foreign' cuts us off from the richness of the world's people, music and languages.
core_ideas.quote: So nationalism is a great diminishment of the self.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay asks: what if the pioneers of Unix and the Internet had branded them 'America Stack'? Would the world have adopted those ideas as readily? Ideas spread best when they don't carry a national flag.
core_ideas.quote: what if they had called it America Stack? Would it have interfered with the willingness of the whole world to accept those brilliant ideas?

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit, mid-explanation of how nations invent a glorious past, notices Ajay grinning and asks 'Why are you smiling?' Ajay: 'Under communism, the future was always certain. It's the past that keeps changing.'

Amit dates English consciousness to the Wars of the Roses, then deadpans that The War of the Roses 'of course, was a 1989 film recently made into a film called The Roses, but that is completely different. Popular culture lovers may not know that it is a tongue in cheek reference to something else that happened.'

On Shudh Hindi sounding like nobody: imagine English speakers using only Latinate words, so that instead of 'we shall fight them in the streets', Winston Churchill had said 'we shall combat them in the boulevards'.

Amit imagines Tagore with modern tech: 'he could have done a YouTube show. Called, and I think he would have called it Everything is Everything. Shob kichu shob kichu.' He also tells Ajay that whatever he says against Bengali economists, 'among Bengali philosophers, Robi-da stands alone.'
After saying it's 'not the ideas of Tagore but those of Putin which will thrive', Amit adds: 'I never thought I'll have those two names in the same sentence.'

Ajay dismantling the word 'Italy': 'Is Italy a football team? That's fine. It's 11 guys that are playing football. Or is Italy the people of Italy? ... Or is it the Italian state? Fine. It is the community that achieves and maintains a monopoly of physical violence on the territory that is Italy.'

Ajay's fix for nationalism in sport: 'form teams based on purely random imagined communities, put a little bit of old fashioned capitalism into it, have buying and selling of players. And you're done.' Amit: in theory every Manchester United player could be playing for Liverpool five years later, 'though it is actually practically impossible because none of them would get into that side.'
On fans picking whichever team was winning when they were 12 or 13: 'Which is why there are chutiyas my age supporting Manchester United. Well, good luck, brother.'

On biryani being treated as anti-national (the 'Ajmal Kasab was given biryani' rhetoric): 'Biryani is not anti national. You're right, it is somewhat unhealthy, but it is deeply, deeply tasty, especially when made well. I am never going to give up biryani.'

Ajay says the universal adoption of blue jeans across India reflects 'some California chic'. Amit corrects him with a 'GK GK': jeans didn't originate in California; the name denim comes from Nîmes in France.
Ajay on data-localisation rhetoric: 'somebody will say data is a new crude oil, which is like supposed to be a checkmate.'
Amit on America's turn to economic nationalism: 'Like we're in a bad video game simulation and there's a bug in the system and something weird just happened.'
Amit on Gandhi walking India barefoot as a tribute to Gokhale: 'I don't know what the logic of that is, but he does that.'
Doug Stanhope on nationalism: 'hating people you have never met and taking pride in accomplishments you had nothing to do with'.
George Orwell's description of sport as 'war minus the shooting', from 'The Sporting Spirit', applied to the India-Pakistan matches.
Ernest Gellner: 'nationalism is not the awakening of nations to self-consciousness. It invents nations where they do not exist.' Paired with Eric Hobsbawm's 'invention of tradition'.
Walt Whitman's 'we contain multitudes', which Amit extends: 'Individuals contain multitudes and multitudes of individuals contain further multitudes.'
Dunbar's number of 150, the natural size of a group where people actually know one another, as the contrast to an 'imagined' national community.
Carl Schmitt: 'politics needs an other'. Nationalism supplies one automatically.

Mussolini, read out by Amit: 'It is not the people who make the state, but the state that makes the people', and 'The fascist conception of the state is all embracing. Outside it no human or spiritual values can exist.'
Hitler's Lebensraum and his use of the 1936 Berlin Olympics to push his nationalist rhetoric.
Ajay: 'if only Vladimir Putin could sign on for Rabindranath Tagore as his spiritual guide instead of Alexander Dugin, then millions of Russians would be alive today.'

Tagore on nationalism: 'a cruel epidemic of evil eating into humanity's moral vitality' and 'the nation, with its flags and pious hymns, cannot hide the fact that the nation is the greatest evil for the earth'. Amit also cites Tagore's view that World War One was caused by the toxic concept of the nation.
Savarkar's test for belonging in India: that it be both your motherland and your holy land. Amit calls it a convenient way to other Christians and Muslims.
Ambedkar calling the Constitution 'a mere topsoil' over a deeper Indian society.
'A language is a dialect with an army', Amit's aside on the many north Indian tongues now dismissed as dialects.
Ajay: 'What you want is the press conferences of Gukesh and Ding'. The gracious world chess championship rivals are the model of sporting conduct.
Amit, arguing that clothes have no religion: 'you didn't think I was gonna quote Dylan here, right? As Bob Dylan once said, even the president of the United States must someday stand naked.'
Ajay recalls, attributing it to Tagore, the wish for 'the winds from the seven continents to blow through my nation'.
